projects.name: Language Models Can Rewrite Their Own Weights
projects.description: arXiv:2611.21885v2 Announce Type: new Abstract: A language model is trained once and frozen. Making it better takes another training run, or a prompt, a harness or extra computation at inference that is gone once the task ends. We show a third way: to our knowledge for the first time, a language model rewrites its own weights by its own reasoning and becomes better, with no gradients and no training. We call this self-rewriting: the model is its own optimizer. In earlier work, a frontier model edited a much smaller one; here an open 27B model, given its weights, its graded answers and the ability to run itself, diagnoses its own failure and rewrites the weights behind it. It surpasses itself: its own edit makes it 6.6 points more accurate on problems it never saw. It keeps getting better: it tests its edits on practice problems and submits only what works, each edit improving on the last, and over eight consecutive sessions its accuracy only rises. It repairs a damaged copy of itself, like a broken robot that fixes itself without being rebuilt: the copy solves almost nothing, yet with no retraining and without ever reading the original weights, the model brings it back to over 80% of the original accuracy on image tasks it never saw. And the ability emerges with scale: in one model family, the smaller models make no edit or break themselves, and only the largest improves and repairs itself. Unlike test-time scaling, self-rewriting writes its gain into the weights, at no cost per answer; unlike training, it runs only forward passes, as serving does. The wall between training and inference is a limit of our tools, not a property of intelligence. We believe self-rewriting is a necessary step toward recursive self-improvement: a model that, like a human, does not separate training from inference could keep upgrading itself for life, with no larger model, no harness or prompt engineering, and no pre- or post-training.

projects.name: An Operationalization of Opaque Serial Depth
projects.description: arXiv:2611.17495v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) is currently a valuable tool for overseeing AI models, but some architectural shifts could significantly reduce CoT monitorability. We find that, across open-weight models, NLS depth correlates strongly with layer count, with some exceptions, and has grown slowly over recent years. projects.name: Benchmarks Don't Talk Back: Learning Through Self-Disagreement
projects.description: arXiv:2611.17563v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A benchmark usually measures a language model alone with a question, and deployment rarely looks like that: answers get contested, and models give up correct ones under counter-reasoning that is itself wrong. We show that what fails there is not a shortfall of accuracy but a capability in its own right -- knowing when to hold a position and when to yield to a better one -- which we call dialectical competence. It stands on first-answer accuracy without following from it: a model can be made materially better at answering and no better at this, and training for accuracy alone can drift against it. Nor can it be bought at inference, by self-reflection or by sampling more. Taking a cue from the dialectical tradition in philosophy, in which productive opposition arises within a position rather than being imposed on it from outside, we hypothesize that this capability can be trained from opposition the model supplies itself. It states a position, generates the strongest case against that position -- its antithesis -- rules on whether the case stands, and is trained on that ruling, with no second model at training or at deployment. We call this learning through Self-Disagreement: reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards throughout, where the same check that scores an answer against its reference scores the ruling too, so no reward model, no preference data and no human annotation enter anywhere. The capability is trained rather than elicited: weak in the base model, it arrives with the reward, is not paid for out of first-answer accuracy, and holds against challengers the model never trained against, including ones stronger than itself. The opposition a model needs in order to improve, it turns out, need not come from outside it.

projects.name: Rational Use of Time for Social Coordination in Humans and AI
projects.description: arXiv:2611.14766v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: All social interactions are situated in time. Previous studies have shown that humans are able to use implicit temporal cues, such as the duration of a pause, to infer others' mental states. projects.name: Robust Task-Aware State Estimation from Pre-trained Perception
projects.description: arXiv:2611.14781v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agents that perform state estimation using pretrained perception models, e.g., Vision-Language Models (VLMs), face the fundamental challenge that predictions are uncertain. Still, most approaches determinize these predictions into a single best-guess state and make decisions as if it were ground truth. This is brittle because when the guess is wrong, the agent's decisions may be unsafe or infeasible. At the other extreme, maintaining a full probability distribution over symbolic states is often intractable. We propose a middle path, drawing on the underlying probabilities the perception model already produces (e.g., a VLM's output-layer token distributions) to construct a $\theta$-confidence Minimal Belief Set (MBS$_\theta$), a minimal subset of states whose cumulative probability meets a user-specified belief-mass threshold. The minimality of an MBS$_\theta$ ensures that the agent considers only the most likely states, enhancing robustness in downstream decision-making while maintaining computational tractability. Using a novel three-layered belief system, we efficiently approximate individual state probabilities from per-feature predictions and task-level constraints. On this belief construction, we base our MBS$_\theta$ construction, while maintaining only a lean factored representation of the belief. Our algorithm, Probability-Ranked Valid State Search (PRaVaSS), takes advantage of the unique structure of this belief system to construct an MBS$_\theta$ with correctness guarantees and polynomial complexity in the unconstrained case. Using a VLM as the backbone of our state estimator, we validate our method's theoretical properties, scalability with problem size, and improvement of downstream decision-making when used in a task-planning pipeline.

projects.name: IntentTwin: Deconfounding Candidate Support and the Oracle-to-Deployment Gap in Offline Web Behavior Prediction
projects.description: arXiv:2611.12918v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Offline web-behavior benchmarks frequently insert the demonstrated action into a finite candidate set and then measure reranking. projects.name: Launch HN: Hamming (YC S24) – Automated Testing for Voice Agents
projects.description:
Hi HN! Sumanyu and Marius here from Hamming (https://www.hamming.ai). Hamming lets you automatically test your LLM voice agent. In our interactive demo, you play the role of the voice agent, and our agent will play the role of a difficult end user. We'll then score your performance on the call. Try it here: https://app.hamming.ai/voice-demo (no signup needed). In practice, our agents call your agent!

LLM voice agents currently require a lot of iteration and tuning. For example, one of our customers is building an LLM drive-through voice agent for fast food chains. Their KPI is order accuracy. It's crucial for their system to gracefully handle dietary restrictions like allergies and customers who get distracted or otherwise change their minds mid-order. Mistakes in this context could lead to unhappy customers, potential health risks, and financial losses.

How do you make sure that such a thing actually works? Most teams spend hours calling their voice agent to find bugs, change the prompt or function definitions, and then call their voice agent again to ensure they fixed the problem and didn't create regressions. This is slow, ad hoc, and feels like a waste of time. In other areas of software development, automated testing has already eliminated this kind of repetitive grunt work — so why not here, too?

We were initially working on helping users create evals for prompts & LLM pipelines for a few months but noticed two things:

1) Many of our friends were building LLM voice agents.

2) They were spending too much time on manual testing.

This gave us evidence that there will be more voice companies in the future, and they will need something to make the iteration process easier. We decided to build it!

Our solution involves four steps:

(1) Create diverse but realistic user personas and scenarios covering the expected conversation space. We create these ourselves for each of our customers. Getting LLMs to create diverse scenarios even with high temperatures is surprisingly tricky. We're learning a lot of tricks along the way to create more randomness and more faithful role-play from the folks at https://www.reddit.com/r/LocalLLaMA/.

(2) Have our agents call your agent when we test your agent's ability to handle things like background noise, long silences, or interruptions. Or have us test just the LLM / logic layer (function calls, etc.) via an API hook.

(3) We score the outputs for each conversation using deterministic checks and LLM judges tailored to the specific problem domain (e.g., order accuracy, tone, friendliness). An LLM judge reviews the entire conversation transcript (including function calls and traces) against predefined success criteria, using examples of both good and bad transcripts as references. It then provides a classification output and detailed reasoning to justify its decisions. Building LLM judges that consistently align with human preferences is challenging, but we're improving with each judge we manually develop.

(4) Re-use the checks and judges above to score production traffic and use it to track quality metrics in production. (i.e., online evals)

We created a Loom recording showing our customers' logged-in experience. We cover how you store and manage scenarios, how you can trigger an experiment run, and how we score each transcript. See the video here: https://www.loom.com/share/839fe585aa1740c0baa4faa33d772d3e

We're inspired by our experiences at Tesla, where Sumanyu led growth initiatives as a data scientist, and Anduril, where Marius headed a data infrastructure team. At both companies, simulations were key to testing autonomous systems before deployment. A common challenge, however, was that simulations often fell short of capturing real-world complexity, resulting in outcomes that didn't always translate to reality. In voice testing, we're optimistic about overcoming this issue. With tools like PlayHT and ElevenLabs, we can generate highly realistic voice interactions, and by integrating LLMs that exhibit human-like reasoning, we hope our simulations will closely replicate how real users interact with voice agents.

For now, we're manually onboarding and activating each user. We're working hard to make it self-serve in the next few weeks. The demo at https://app.hamming.ai/voice-demo doesn't require any signup, though!

Our current pricing is a mix of usage and the number of seats: https://hamming.ai/pricing. We don't use customer data for training purposes or to benefit other customers, and we don't sell any data. We use PostHog to track usage. We're in the process of getting HIPAA compliance, with SOC 2 being next on the list.

Looking ahead, we're focused on making scenario generation and LLM judge creation more automated and self-serve. We also want to create personas based on real production conversations to make it easier to ‘replay’ a user on demand.

A natural next step beyond testing is optimization. We're considering building a voice agent optimizer (like DSPy) that uses scenarios from testing that failed to generate a new set of prompts or function call definitions to make the scenario pass. We find the potential of self-play and self-improvement here super exciting.

We'd love to hear about your experiences with voice agents, whether as a user or someone building them. If you're building in the voice or agentic space, we're curious about what is working well for you and what challenges you are encountering. We're eager to learn from your insights about setting up evals and simulation pipelines or your thoughts on where this space is heading.

projects.name: Rethinking in Spikes: Mitigating Hallucinations in MDLMs with Step-Aware Decoding
projects.description: arXiv:2611.12901v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent advancements in multimodal diffusion language models (MDLMs) have exhibited strong global modeling capabilities through iterative refinement. We hypothesize that discrete token commitment discards the distributional information at masked positions, limiting the continued interaction between candidate semantics and the context during entropy spikes. With this goal, we present StepRefine, a plug-and-play decoding strategy that leverages semantic context to achieve reliable denoising. The core of our method lies in a step-aware switch between discrete denoising and latent refinement. The model employs probability-weighted embeddings at entropy spike steps to preserve diverse reasoning hypotheses and performs multiple rounds of continuous refinement. Meanwhile, a refinement controller monitors distributional stability to reduce unnecessary loops and switch the model back to standard discrete denoising. Through extensive experiments, StepRefine demonstrates significant hallucination mitigation across different MDLMs on multimodal benchmarks.

projects.name: SELD: Detecting Silent Evidence Loss in Context Compression beyond the Answer
projects.description: arXiv:2611.12903v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Context compression is now routine for language models with long inputs, but a compressed context is useful only if it keeps the evidence for the answer. In one direction, the TSFM encodes the series in compressed form for the LLM, which reasons over it together with the text. In the other, the LLM's reasoning is fed back into the TSFM, which produces the forecast conditioned on it. One model architecture thus reads and generates both series and text, reasons in text, and draws on the TSFM's pretrained forecasting ability. projects.name: khammoon: From a Linguistic Guideline to a Thai Morpheme Segmenter
projects.description: arXiv:2611.13012v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Thai is written without spaces between words, making segmentation a foundational step in most Thai NLP pipelines. Segmenting at the morphemic level provides an explicit, consistent morphological representation that eliminates compounding ambiguity. Finally, we train khammoon, a lightweight 1M-parameter convolutional BiLSTM segmenter designed for efficient CPU inference, achieving a boundary F1 of 0.992 on out-of-domain text. The guideline, datasets, model, and library are all publicly released.

projects.name: Compression of Emotion in Language Model Representations
projects.description: arXiv:2611.08683v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have been evaluated on their ability to identify emotions expressed in text and produce fluent emotional language. projects.name: Contextuality and Contradictions: Exploring Real-World Identifications of AI-Generated Writing
projects.description: arXiv:2611.08704v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As AI-generated content spreads into nearly every domain of human interaction, practices and discourses of AI detection, both formal and informal, have become an everyday part of how people interact with text and with each other. In this paper, we explore the real-world practices and discourses of AI identification that have emerged in response to a shifting discursive landscape where the human provenance of a text can no longer be taken for granted. We pair qualitative coding with computational analysis of lexical change, grounded in linguistic anthropological perspectives on language and communication, to investigate AI identifications among English Wikipedia editors and students. We find that these identifications draw on a diversity of evidentiary types, from discrete textual features and judgments about content to circular sense-making claims and presumptions about the author's moral character, and that they are contradictory, dynamic, and contextually dependent. In practice, what often motivates an AI identification is not the presence of any specific textual element, but pragmatic infelicity: a perceived mismatch between the elements present and those deemed appropriate within the text's particular context. Consequently, real-world identifications of AI-generated writing do not merely neutrally point out the perceived presence of "AI-like" features, but can be leveraged as a discursive resource to maintain and define sociolinguistic norms: what can be said in a given context, what is appropriate, and, ultimately, what is human. Further, the design and implementation of systems and tools that treat AI-likeness as a context-free property of text may therefore inherit, and enforce at scale, the norms of whichever contexts they were trained on.

projects.name: FinEvolveKG: Controlled and Attributable Prompt Evolution for Financial Knowledge Graph Construction
projects.description: arXiv:2611.08643v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Financial institutions construct knowledge graphs (KGs) from shared SEC 10-Ks to serve risk analysis, portfolio management, and investment research, whose analytical needs differ. projects.name: Forcing a Letter Suppresses Refusal: Mechanistic Evidence from WMDP
projects.description: arXiv:2611.08639v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Safety benchmarks for large language models (LLMs) commonly use multiple-choice question (MCQ) format. Moreover, ablating the attention heads that carry the MCQ format answer increases the refusal, which is a direct evidence that the MCQ answer-selection competes with refusal. These findings indicate that MCQ safety scores primarily measure knowledge capabilities and do not assess the safety-mechanisms.

projects.name: From Procedures to Permissions: Learning Precise Subagent Authorization from Agent Skills
projects.description: arXiv:2611.08905v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As language agents tackle increasingly complex tasks, they increasingly rely on multiple agents to coordinate specialized work, requiring decisions not only about what each subagent should do but also which tools and workspace resources it should access. On Terminal-Bench 2.1 and SkillsBench, our method remains competitive with existing agent data synthesis approaches. These results show that the procedural knowledge embedded in Agent Skills provides a source of supervision for precise subagent orchestration that task outcomes alone cannot provide.

projects.description: arXiv:2611.08780v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The number of domain fine-tuned models, particularly in the biomedical domain, is rapidly expanding. projects.description: arXiv:2611.08892v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recursive self-training of language models, a setting studied in model collapse, can reduce vocabulary while making frequent words, mostly function words, less dominant. projects.name: Semantic Conditional Similarity (SCS): A Formal Mathematical Framework
projects.description: arXiv:2611.08778v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Semantic Textual Similarity (STS) operates on document pairs, returning a single scalar per comparison. In a multi-document setting where several sources may have contributed to one or more targets, pairwise STS cannot disentangle each source's marginal semantic contribution from their shared vocabulary. In this paper, Semantic Conditional Similarity (SCS) is introduced as a conditional form of STS that computes similarity between two documents after eliminating semantic elements shared with a third via set-theoretic operations. SCS makes four contributions: 1) it introduces directionality, partitioning pairwise relations into lateral (inter-source) and vertical (source-to-target) classes; 2) conditioning induces role-dependent asymmetry by extending the comparison domain from unordered pairs to ordered, conditioned triples of a target, a reference, and a conditioning document; 3) SCS introduces inter-document conditioning by subtracting shared content from a third document, complementing the intra-document conditioning in recent C-STS work; and 4) the set-theoretic decomposition achieves threshold-free partitioning of shared and residual content, requiring no arbitrary similarity cutoff. Although developed for the $n \to 1$ configuration, the framework extends to $1 \to n$ via vertical role reversal and to $m \to n$ via independent composition of source- and target-side conditioning. With the established $1 \to 1$ case, these span the full spectrum of document cardinality. SCS scores should be interpreted ordinally, as rankings of marginal contributions rather than absolute measurements. The broader implication is that metric space axioms commonly assumed in similarity formalizations constrain expressiveness in role-differentiated multi-document settings, and that extending the domain to conditioned triples can recover information that pairwise-symmetric comparisons suppress.
